name: 02-ensembles
title: Simulation Ensembles — systematic perturbation and comparative physiology

parent_studies.rationale: Ensembles sweep the interchangeable spec across severity and engine.

question:
Can the simulation core run the sepsis model as an ENSEMBLE — many configurations
(severity × engine) executed as one orchestrated batch and gathered into a single
comparison?
claim:
The sepsis core runs as a severity {0,1,3} × engine {BioGears, Tellurium, surrogate}
ensemble, gathered into one grid. The two full-physics engines agree to within ~0.1% and
show the expected severity response (minimum tissue integrity 1.00 healthy -> 0.97
mild -> 0.24 severe); their heavy runs are cited from the committed severity studies.
The surrogate ran live across every cell in the same batch — the orchestration proof
that the harness executes many cheap configurations in one sweep — and is flagged a
fast approximate tier (its endpoint is out of physical range; its real contribution,
speed, is study 04).

findings.summary: One batch, severity × engine — the full-physics engines show the severity response and agree.
findings.detail:
Minimum tissue integrity (the inflammation core) across severities {0,1,3}:
BioGears and the exact Tellurium extraction both fall 1.00 (healthy) -> 0.968
(mild) -> 0.243 (severe), to within ~0.1%. These are the committed heavy runs from the
severity studies (01/02/03), assembled here as one ensemble grid — the same shape
the batch harness produces for any registered engine.

findings.summary: The surrogate ran live across every cell — the orchestration proof.
findings.detail:
In the same batch the PyTorch surrogate was swept across all three severities
live (seconds total), demonstrating that the orchestration runs many cheap
configurations in one sweep. The surrogate is a fast APPROXIMATE tier: its
tissue-integrity endpoint is out of physical range (accuracy is data-limited),
so it is reported for transparency but not presented as a science value. Its
real contribution is speed (study 04); its honest fidelity picture is study 05.
findings.statement: The surrogate's divergence from the full-physics engines is a difference in tier, not a rival prediction. One batch answers a fidelity question and an orchestration question side by side.
findings.explanation:
The batch makes two different kinds of claim, and the apparent divergence sits entirely at the boundary between them. BioGears and the exact Tellurium extraction — two independently built full-physics engines — agree to within ~0.1% on minimum tissue integrity across severities {0,1,3} (1.00 healthy -> 0.968 mild -> 0.243 severe). Because they are separate implementations, that agreement is cross-engine replication: the severity response is a property of the shared model, not an artifact of one engine. That is the fidelity claim this study supports.

The surrogate is a different tier. Its tissue-integrity endpoint is out of physical range, so it is not a third physical estimate competing with the full-physics pair; reading it that way would be wrong. Its presence in every cell proves only what it is meant to: the harness orchestrates many cheap configurations in one sweep (the throughput claim, quantified in study 04). The divergence is by design, not an unresolved contradiction. The full-physics engines answer 'does the model show the expected, engine-independent severity response?' (yes); the surrogate answers 'can the batch harness fan a cheap engine across the whole grid live?' (yes). Neither bears on the other.

The open question the divergence makes visible is whether the surrogate can be moved from orchestration-proof to a science-grade tier at all. This grid cannot decide that; it needs a held-out quantitative fidelity test for the surrogate against the full-physics endpoints, which is the work deferred to study 05. Until that test exists, the surrogate's number stays reported for transparency and excluded from any fidelity claim.
